claims.text: The wear resistance of HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by their nanoscale grain structure.
Refining the nanocrystalline microstructure enhances dynamic strain hardening during wear.
Grain refinement promotes grain-boundary-mediated dislocation pile-up and accommodation.
The baseline coating has an average grain size of approximately 20 nm and receives no post-deposition thermal processing.
A controlled post-deposition thermal treatment can reduce the average grain size from approximately 20 nm to approximately 10–15 nm without phase transformation or coarsening.
Grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion in these coatings.
The increased grain-boundary density promotes dynamic strain hardening under wear loading.
Enhanced dynamic strain hardening increases resistance to material removal by abrasive or adhesive wear.
Thermally treated coatings with 10–15 nm grains should have a lower wear rate than untreated coatings with approximately 20 nm grains.
Wear resistance should be greatest in an optimal grain-size range around 10–15 nm.
The proposed grain-size effect should hold across HEA coatings having similar high-configurational-entropy alloying strategies.
Below approximately 5 nm, the wear-resistance benefit may diminish because grain-boundary sliding can dominate.
Above approximately 50 nm, the proposed effect may diminish because conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity prevails.
The exact wear improvement and thermal-processing parameters required for optimal refinement are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear-rate reduction or a concomitant increase in dynamic hardness relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
